_note: Indirect fire. The mortar firing table is a community measurement, not a published one, and it is the most contested number in WARDOGS artillery. Every figure here says where it came from and how much to trust it. Nothing is invented to fill a gap: the SPH-2 tables are transcribed from the one calculator that publishes a complete curve, and they are marked unfired until somebody checks a row in game.

grid.note: The game's own X/Y. One unit is 100 m, so 0.01 is a metre. Y counts north.

platforms.name: L81 Mortar
notes: One trajectory. The barrel will not come down past a steep angle, so past the elevation that throws furthest every extra mil lands the shell shorter, and there is a dead circle around the gun that cannot be hit from that position at all. Move the mortar rather than keep dialling.

The table is monotonic and, from 290 to 690 mil, exactly one metre lost per mil gained. That regularity may be real or may be two measured endpoints with the middle interpolated. It is a starting point; range the first shell.

platforms.name: SPH-2
platforms.tableSource: wardogs-artillery.com, the only source that publishes the complete curve. Transcribed 2026-08-30, not yet checked against the game.
notes: Two trajectories. The low arc reaches from 1181 m to maximum range and arrives sooner; below that the high arc is the only one that reaches at all. From 1181 m out, both arcs reach and both solutions are reported.

Past about 2625 m the arc turns over and the table goes flat: a metre of extra range costs a great deal of elevation, and two different elevations both land. Do not fight for the last hundred metres, move the gun.
The published table continues one row past the stated envelope, to 735 m at 1400 mil. That row sits outside the envelope the other sources agree on, so it is left out here.
The tagged expensive 155mm is a different projectile, a fraction of the mass and drag, and would need its own table. Whether the SPH-2 can load it is unsettled.

caveats: The firing table is flat ground. It assumes the gun and the target sit at the same height, and the terrain is a river valley with ridges. A shot from the valley floor onto high ground falls short of this; a shot down off a ridge carries past.

Grouping is an angle, so the error grows with range. A mortar at the far end of its reach puts shells across about ten metres whatever you dial, which is why the first round is a ranging round and not the shot.
What the grouping angle bounds is not stated anywhere: a radius, a full width or a typical spread. Read the number as the scale of the error, not a guarantee.

open.what: The SPH-2 table is transcribed, not fired
open.why: wardogs-artillery.com is the one source publishing the complete curve for both arcs, and no second source confirms it. It is carried here with that label rather than left out, because a labelled single source beats a gap.
open.close: Fire three rows and compare: one mid low arc near 2000 m, one on the flat top near 2625 m, and one below 1181 m where only the high arc reaches. If all three land, trust the curve.

open.what: No time of flight for either platform
open.why: Two calculators mention it, neither publishes numbers. Without it you cannot lead a moving target or judge whether a target will still be there.
open.close: Time from the round leaving the tube to impact, at three or four ranges per platform. It is a stopwatch job, not a derivation.

open.why: The terrain is a river valley with ridges, so a shot up onto high ground falls short and a shot down off a ridge carries past. This is the largest accuracy gap on the page, bigger than the grouping.
open.close: Fire at a target with a known height difference and record how far the fall of shot moves per metre of elevation change. One coefficient per platform would cover most of it.

open.what: The mortar's maximum range is contested
open.why: Three community sources say roughly 680 to 700 m, one says 3.1 km. This site uses the short figure.
open.close: Early Access on 10 September 2026. One shot at maximum elevation settles it.

open.what: The mortar's mil envelope disagrees between sources
open.why: The table used here runs 290 to 900 mil. Another calculator publishes 150 to 850 mil for the same weapon, so at least one of the two is reading a different scale off the gun.
open.close: Note what the sight actually reads at maximum and minimum elevation.

open.what: Part of the mortar table may be interpolated rather than measured
open.why: From 290 to 690 mil it is exactly one metre lost per mil gained across nine consecutive rows. That regularity is either the real design or two measured endpoints with the middle filled in.
open.close: Spot check one middle row, say 500 m, against the game.

dispute.detail: Three independent community calculators put it between roughly 680 and 700 m: 110 to 700 m, 132 to 684 m, and about 120 to 700 m. One publishes 3.1 km for the same weapon. Nothing is official either way, but three measurements agreeing to within a few percent against one outlier is not a coin flip, so this site uses the short figure and says why.
